newsitem.title: USA: Electoral college - odd key to White House door.
newsitem.headline: Electoral college - odd key to White House door.

text.p: An odd ritual will unfurl across America on Tuesday when millions of citizens cast votes for utter strangers, creating a "college" that exists in name only, which will pick the next president of the United States.
It's the American way of electing a national leader.
It drives people crazy.

The indirect election system enshrined in the Constitution requires that presidents be chosen not by popular vote but by an Electoral College of 538 members distributed roughly according to populace among the 50 states and Washington, D.C.

When someone casts a vote for Democratic President Bill Clinton, Republican nominee Bob Dole or a minor party candidate on November 5, the vote goes not to them but to their local representatives called electors.
In some states the candidates' names do not even appear on the ballot. One votes merely for a party slate.
And the electors never meet as a "college." They gather in their own state capitals on a legally fixed day -- Dec. 18 this year -- to vote for president and vice president.
They are not even legally bound to back the candidates to whom they are pledged, although mutinies are very rare.
A simple majority of 270 votes wins.
Those are the basics of an odd, elitist system invented by the New World aristocrats who wrote the Constitution in 1787.
They feared a populace of backwoods bumpkins would pick leaders unwisely and envisioned the electors as a panel of wise men who could be trusted to make an enlightened final choice.

The advent of political parties quashed that idea. Today the statewide slates of elector-candidates are named by the parties or campaign bosses, who reward political stalwarts and expect them to vote as they are pledged.

There has been some other tinkering with the system over the years. But real democratic reform has fizzled because of politics, the difficulty of amending the Constitution and the short life of good intentions.

And so America remains a political checkerboard of separate and unequal battlegrounds in which -- as reformers never tire of noting -- a candidate could lose the popular vote, lose most of the states and still win the White House.
That stems from the unequal distribution of electors: Each state gets the same number as its congressional contingent of senators and representatives, so the bigger the state the bigger the prize.
California has the biggest bloc with 54 electoral votes. Seven states and Washington, D.C., have only three each.
Whoever gets the most popular votes in a state gets all of its electoral votes. That creates a potential distortion between national popular vote and electoral vote.
The winner in California, for example, can lose the 19 smallest states and still be even.
The only exceptions to the winner-take-all rule are Maine and Nebraska, where it is possible to split electoral winnings under some circumstances. But they share only nine votes.
Critics have no end of fun with electoral arithmetic. For instance, a candidate could in theory lose 39 states and still win by taking just the top 11. They have 270 votes.
Gerald Ford beat Jimmy Carter in 27 states in 1976 but Carter gathered bigger electoral prizes and won.
The odds against winning the presidency in defiance of the national popular will are long, but three men have done it. The last was Benjamin Harrison in 1888.

The system does prevent political paralysis when there are strong third-party candidates and no one wins a popular majority. Richard Nixon in 1968 and Clinton in 1992 both won with only 43 percent support in a three-way field.
The system provides for the House of Representatives to decide the winner if no one wins an electoral majority. That has happened only twice, in 1801 and 1825.
A final quirk is the possibility of the "faithless elector" who ignores his pledge and votes for someone else.
But only seven have done so in this century -- the last in 1988 when many Democrats wished their ticket had been Lloyd Bentsen-Michael Dukakis instead of the reverse.
Margaret Leach, a Dukakis elector from West Virginia, acted out their fantasy by voting for Bentsen, so that the record will always read: Bush 426, Dukakis 111, Other 1.
